module.title: Days 1–10 | Competition Mastery Module
module.description: Production candidate: authored topic-driven Computer Challenge curriculum.

lessons.title: Computer fundamentals and hardware
lessons.objective: Explain how core computer components work together to accept input, process information, store data and produce output.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A computer system combines hardware and software. Input devices provide data, the processor executes instructions, memory holds data needed during active work, and storage keeps information persistently. Output devices present results. Performance questions often require distinguishing temporary working memory from long-term storage and identifying the role of each component in a system.
examples: A keyboard supplies input, the CPU processes instructions, RAM holds active data and programs, an SSD stores files persistently, and a display presents visual output.

A keyboard supplies input, the CPU processes instructions, RAM holds active data and programs, an SSD stores files persistently, and a display presents visual output. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.
lessons.practical_activity: Label the input, processing, memory, storage and output stages for three everyday computing tasks.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded Computer Challenge problems for Computer fundamentals and hardware: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent reasoning on the third. Ask the learner to state the evidence or rule used before confirming the answer.
independent_practice: Match components to functions
Distinguish RAM from storage
Identify an input device and output device
Predict which component is relevant to a stated task.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item hardware checkpoint with at least six correct functional matches.
lessons.student_task: Create a labelled block diagram showing how data moves through a computer system.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Ask learners to distinguish closely related computing concepts before answering. Encourage diagrams, traces and evidence-based diagnosis instead of memorised labels. The sequence remains suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Explain why turning off a computer can remove information from RAM while files remain on storage.

lessons.title: Operating systems and files
lessons.objective: Use operating-system concepts to manage files, folders, applications and permissions safely and logically.
lessons.core_teaching_content: An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services for applications and users. Files are stored in folders and identified by names and formats. Extensions often indicate the type of content or application associated with a file. Good file management uses meaningful names, predictable folders, backups and appropriate permissions rather than relying on the desktop as permanent storage.
examples: A project folder might contain separate folders for source files, exported documents and backups, making retrieval and version control easier.

A project folder might contain separate folders for source files, exported documents and backups, making retrieval and version control easier. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Data representation and storage
lessons.objective: Explain how computers represent, store and move digital information and apply basic binary reasoning.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Computers represent information using discrete states. Binary uses two symbols, 0 and 1, and combinations of bits can represent numbers and encoded information. Larger units such as bytes group bits. Text, images, audio and other media require encoding and storage formats. A larger file may require more storage or bandwidth, but the exact size depends on representation and compression.
examples: Eight binary bits form one byte. The decimal number 5 is represented as 00000101 in an eight-bit unsigned representation.

Eight binary bits form one byte. The decimal number 5 is represented as 00000101 in an eight-bit unsigned representation. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Networks and internet fundamentals
lessons.objective: Explain how devices communicate across networks and distinguish local networking, internet services and common addressing concepts.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A network connects devices so they can exchange data and share resources. Local networks connect nearby devices, while the internet is an interconnected global network. Routers forward traffic between networks; switches connect devices within a local network. Domain names provide human-readable names that resolve through DNS to network addresses. Reliable answers distinguish a service from the device or protocol delivering it.
examples: A home router can connect phones and computers to a local network and provide a path to internet services, while DNS helps translate a website name into an address.

A home router can connect phones and computers to a local network and provide a path to internet services, while DNS helps translate a website name into an address. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity and safe digital behaviour
lessons.objective: Recognise common cybersecurity threats and choose practical controls that reduce account, device and data risk.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Cybersecurity protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. Common threats include phishing, credential theft, malicious software, unsafe links and weak authentication. Strong unique passwords, multi-factor authentication, software updates, backups and cautious handling of links and attachments reduce risk. Security decisions should consider both the threat and the control that addresses it.
examples: A convincing message asking for an urgent password reset may be phishing. Checking the destination independently rather than using the embedded link reduces the risk of credential theft.

A convincing message asking for an urgent password reset may be phishing. Checking the destination independently rather than using the embedded link reduces the risk of credential theft. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Productivity, data and digital workflows
lessons.objective: Use structured digital workflows to create, organise, analyse and present information accurately.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Productivity software supports documents, spreadsheets, presentations and structured data. Good workflows separate raw data from calculated results, use clear labels and validate inputs before drawing conclusions. Spreadsheets are useful for repeated calculations and sorting, while documents and presentations communicate conclusions. Accuracy depends on checking formulas, units, dates and source information rather than trusting formatting alone.
examples: A spreadsheet can calculate totals from raw scores, but the formula and source values should be checked before publishing a ranking.

A spreadsheet can calculate totals from raw scores, but the formula and source values should be checked before publishing a ranking. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Algorithms and computational thinking
lessons.objective: Break problems into precise steps, identify patterns and conditions, and compare simple algorithms for correctness and efficiency.
lessons.core_teaching_content: An algorithm is a finite sequence of instructions for solving a problem. Computational thinking uses decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design. Conditions allow decisions, loops repeat actions, and variables store changing values. A correct algorithm produces the intended result for valid inputs; efficiency considers how much work or resource it needs.
examples: To find the largest of three numbers, initialise a current maximum, compare each value, and replace the maximum when a larger value appears.

To find the largest of three numbers, initialise a current maximum, compare each value, and replace the maximum when a larger value appears. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting and systems reasoning
lessons.objective: Diagnose common computer problems by gathering evidence, isolating causes and applying the least risky appropriate fix.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Troubleshooting should be systematic rather than random. Define the symptom, reproduce it safely, check simple causes first, change one relevant factor at a time, and verify the result. Consider power, connectivity, configuration, software state and hardware. Keep records of changes so a failed intervention can be reversed. Escalate when the issue involves permissions, sensitive data or hardware risk beyond the user's role.
examples: If a computer cannot access one website but other sites work, checking the site, browser, DNS and network path is more informative than immediately reinstalling the operating system.

If a computer cannot access one website but other sites work, checking the site, browser, DNS and network path is more informative than immediately reinstalling the operating system. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.

lessons.title: Integrated computer mini-mock
lessons.objective: Apply hardware, software, networking, cybersecurity, data and algorithm concepts under timed competition conditions and convert errors into targeted revision.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A strong computer-competition attempt requires switching between conceptual knowledge, diagrams, data representation, algorithms and cybersecurity scenarios. Read every question for the exact task and eliminate options that confuse related concepts. After the attempt, classify mistakes as knowledge gaps, misread requirements, reasoning errors or careless execution. Revision should target the observed error pattern.
examples: A question about a slow application may involve memory, storage, network access or software state; the best answer depends on the evidence supplied rather than a memorised claim that one component is always responsible.

A question about a slow application may involve memory, storage, network access or software state; the best answer depends on the evidence supplied rather than a memorised claim that one component is always responsible. Apply the same concept to a different computing scenario and require the learner to justify the choice.
lessons.practical_activity: Complete a mixed timed set, record uncertain items and review each error using an evidence-first diagnosis.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded Computer Challenge problems for Integrated computer mini-mock: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent reasoning on the third. Ask the learner to state the evidence or rule used before confirming the answer.
independent_practice: Answer one hardware, one networking, one binary, one cybersecurity, one algorithm and one troubleshooting item
Explain the principle behind each answer.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an integrated checkpoint and record accuracy, time, guessed items and error categories.
lessons.student_task: Create a one-page Computer Challenge revision plan with three strengths, three gaps and one measurable next-attempt target.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Ask learners to distinguish closely related computing concepts before answering. Encourage diagrams, traces and evidence-based diagnosis instead of memorised labels. The sequence remains suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Identify the error category with the greatest improvement opportunity and define one concrete practice action.
